extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) involved in obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and supporting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including how to identify teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine, reasonable expectation of success, claim construction considerations, and use of legal and technical rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching/Suggestion/Motivation requirement to modify or combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Then, Office personnel must articulate the following: (1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings; (2) a finding that there was reasonable expectation of success; and (3) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must explicitly state these findings in the rejection; if any cannot be made, the rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: combining Asano with an electronic sensor; updating password device with bioauthentication. Reference case law (DyStar, Kahn, KSR) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine may be explicit or implicit
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have made clear that the teaching, suggestion, or motivation test is flexible and an explicit suggestion to combine the prior art is not necessary. The motivation to combine may be implicit and may be found in the knowledge of one of ordinary skill in the art, or, in some cases, from the nature of the problem to be solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit motivations include market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings, any need/problem known in the field, and background knowledge/common sense of a person of ordinary skill. Cite Zup v. Nash Mfg., Plantronics v. Aliph, Perfect Web Techs., and KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirable alternatives in prior art do not necessarily teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of desirable alternatives does not necessarily negate a suggestion for modifying the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere disclosure of more than one alternative is not teaching away unless the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution. Example: In re Fulton — disclosure of multiple orientations did not teach away from the claimed facing orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh suggestive power where prior art teachings conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the teachings of two or more prior art references conflict, the examiner must weigh the power of each reference to suggest solutions to one of ordinary skill in the art, considering the degree to which one reference might accurately discredit another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider differences in conditions, relevance, experimental comparability (see In re Young example). Do not automatically discard a reference because of later conflicting literature without assessing comparability and persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere possibility of combination is insufficient without predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that references can be combined or modified does not render the resultant combination obvious unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply KSR: predictable variations that a skilled artisan could implement likely render unpatentable; unpredictable arts require more than mere suggestion. Use factual explanation showing predictability in the specific context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions of obviousness require articulated reasoning (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that modifications of the prior art would have been ‘well within the ordinary skill of the art’ or similar conclusory statements are not sufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness without some objective reason to combine the teachings of the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide an articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (KSR, In re Kahn). Avoid mere conclusory assertions; explain why a person of ordinary skill would combine references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification must not render the prior art unsatisfactory for its intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed modification would render the prior art invention being modified unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there may be no suggestion or motivation to make the proposed modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the modification would make the reference inoperable or ineffective for its intended use (see In re Gordon). Consider whether claimed benefits of primary reference would be lost; if so, may teach away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification must not change the principle of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed modification or combination of the prior art would change the principle of operation of the prior art invention being modified, then the teachings of the references are not sufficient to render the claims prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require showing that combination does not require substantial reconstruction or redesign or a change in basic operating principle (see In re Ratti). If change of principle required, explain why combination is not appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is a reason to modify or combine the prior art to achieve the claimed invention, the claims may be rejected as prima facie obvious provided there is also a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation of success refers to the likelihood that the combination/modification would meet claim limitations. It can be shown implicitly via prior art teachings but should be indicated explicitly in the rejection. Cite Elekta v. ZAP, Intelligent Bio-Sys., In re Merck examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some degree of predictability is required; lack of predictability can support nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness does not require absolute predictability, but at least some degree of predictability is required. Evidence showing there was no reasonable expectation of success may support a conclusion of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider field predictability (e.g., highly unpredictable biotech/therapeutics). Use contemporaneous evidence demonstrating unpredictability (OSI Pharm., Amgen, In re Rinehart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability/expectation of success determined at the relevant time
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an art is predictable or whether the proposed modification or combination of the prior art has a reasonable expectation of success is determined at the time the invention was made (pre-AIA) or before the effective filing date (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame analysis with correct temporal reference depending on statute and application effective date. Use contemporaneous prior art and knowledge, not later data.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art. Examiners must consider all claim limitations when determining patentability of an invention over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply correct claim construction (broadest reasonable interpretation for examination context). Avoid improperly narrowing claim scope to preferred embodiments (see Axonics v. Medtronic). Consider whether grammar/ordinary meaning renders a term limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite claim limitations cannot be disregarded
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation which is considered indefinite cannot be disregarded. If a claim is subject to more than one interpretation, at least one of which would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, the examiner should reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and should reject the claim over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base a prior art rejection on speculative or unreasonable claim interpretations. If appropriate, make both an indefiniteness rejection and a prior art rejection to avoid piecemeal appeals (Ex parte Ionescu, In re Steele).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations lacking support in original specification must still be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating claims for obviousness, all the limitations of the claims must be considered and given weight, including limitations which do not find support in the specification as originally filed (i.e., new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore negative or other limitations absent from the original spec when assessing prior art (Ex parte Grasselli, In re Miller). Consider whether the limitation is part of properly construed claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale to combine may be found in references, common knowledge, scientific principles, or legal precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to modify or combine the prior art does not have to be expressly stated in the prior art; it may be expressly or impliedly contained in the prior art or it may be reasoned from knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art, established scientific principles, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may rely on legal precedent or art-recognized equivalents when appropriate but must provide convincing line of reasoning and apply these rationales to the facts at hand (In re Fine, In re Jones, In re Kotzab, Ex parte Clapp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of some advantage is the strongest rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation of some advantage is the strongest rationale for combining references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing motivation to combine, emphasize predictable advantages (stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, smaller, more durable, more efficient). Show how advantages would motivate a skilled artisan to combine teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat common rationales as per se rules; explain applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel are cautioned against treating any line of reasoning as a per se rule. Automating a manual activity, making portable, making separable, reversing or duplicating parts, or purifying an old product may form the basis of a rejection but should not be treated as per se rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explanation of how such a rationale applies to the particular facts; mere invocation of a principle (e.g., 'art recognized similarity') without application to facts is generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims and claim scope relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. However, this may not apply if a dependent claim is not properly dependent or has a later effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider effective filing dates on a claim-by-claim basis and ensure proper dependency; consult MPEP §§ 608.01(n), 2133.01, and 2152.01 for effective filing date issues.
